body: Lakonishok & Lee, 'Are Insider Trades Informative?' (Review of Financial Studies 14(1):79-111, 2001; NYSE/AMEX/Nasdaq 1975-1995): the market barely reacts when insiders trade or report, yet insider activity predicts future returns; the informativeness comes from PURCHASES, selling has no predictive ability, and the effect is driven by smaller firms. Insiders in aggregate are contrarian and time the market better than simple contrarian rules. Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski, 'Decoding Inside Information' (Journal of Finance 67(3):1009-1043, 2012; 1986-2007): classify an insider as 'routine' if they traded in the same calendar month in each of the prior three years; everyone else is 'opportunistic'. A portfolio following only opportunistic trades earns value-weighted abnormal returns of ~82 bp/month (~10%/yr); routine trades earn essentially zero. Most informative: local, non-executive insiders at geographically concentrated, poorly governed firms; opportunistic traders also attract more SEC enforcement. Practical rule: weight open-market buys (code P) by non-routine insiders, multiple insiders, size of buy vs. their holdings/salary, and small/under-covered firms; ignore grants, exercises, and calendar-regular trades. Signal is public within 2 business days - edge comes from filtering, not speed.

data.ll2001: purchases informative, sales not, small firms drive it
data.routine_definition: traded same month in each of prior 3 years

title: Insider BUYING predicts returns (esp. small caps, opportunistic insiders); selling mostly doesn't
